en.title: Nov 16–22 | This Week’s Top AI Papers
en.summary: Can agents accumulate experience on their own, improve their skills, and get cheaper to run the more they're used? This edition's 10 selected AI papers—spanning everything from letting AI remember the gains and losses of each edit and automatically monitoring training, to streamlining Skills and reviewing high-risk updates—focus on "how to make agents keep improving." Anyone building Agents or following AI research should take a close look at the practical ideas inside.
en.reason: Google DeepMind, Google Cloud AI and Penn State's SIM optimizer uses memory to fix a 68.41-vs-73.89 drop after Opus-to-Gemini migration and improve 9 of 10 coding experiments by 2.36 points (p=0.003), one of 10 papers on agents learning from experience.

The weekend’s biggest news wasn’t a US stock market crash—it was AI claiming to prove the Riemann Hypothesis

This weekend, what truly shook the world was not the sharp selloff in US stocks but news from the math world: on November 20, Levent Alpöge, a 34-year-old mathematician at Anthropic, posted a statement on his personal website saying he had worked with the company’s large model Claude to find a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, which has puzzled mathematicians for 167 years, and that the method could be extended to the stronger Generalized Riemann Hypothesis.
en.summary:
The biggest news this weekend wasn't a US stock market crash — it was AI "proving" the Riemann Hypothesis

What truly shook the world this weekend wasn't the sharp slide in US stocks, but a message from the world of mathematics: on November 20, Levent Alpöge, a 34-year-old mathematician at Anthropic, posted a statement on his personal website saying that he had worked with the company's large model Claude to find a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, which has vexed mathematicians for 167 years, and that the method could be extended to the stronger Generalized Riemann Hypothesis.

The news instantly ignited not just the math world but the entire capital market — after all, Anthropic had just completed the largest IPO in history, listing on Nasdaq on November 19, and the statement came out exactly one day later. Alpöge himself admitted the timing was "terrible."

Why call it "earth-shattering…

en.title: 🏆 The top spot on the coding agent leaderboard has changed hands — should you switch tools right away?
en.summary:
🏆 There's a new No. 1 on the coding agent leaderboard — should you switch tools right away?

Don't just look at the ranking.

Google's @_mohansolo says Neon, paired with their own Antigravity command line (AGY CLI), now tops the AA coding agent index; he also noted that a big part of the gain came from the harness (the orchestration shell).

That point is worth remembering more than the ranking itself: same model, different harness, and the score can differ by a noticeable margin. So before switching tools, I look at four things:

1. Whether the leaderboard is measuring the "model" or the "model plus a particular harness." If your harness is different, the scores may not carry over.

2. Run real tasks in your own repo for a week and note how often you have to redo the work.

3. Check quotas and pricing. A single agent run is tens of thousands of toke…
en.reason: Google's @_mohansolo says Neon with the Antigravity CLI (AGY CLI) now tops the AA coding agent index, with much of the gain coming from the harness, so the piece argues the same model can score differently under another shell and lists four checks before switching tools.

en.title: OpenAI really could collapse in the short term.
en.summary:
OpenAI really could collapse in the short term.

There are quite a few reasons, and whether they add up to the collapse threshold is a matter of luck.

Maybe YES, maybe NO.

The first point, and the most fatal one, is that Altman doesn't observe financial discipline. Last October, bypassing chip suppliers like NVDA and Google, he went straight to South Korea to ask for HBM, which directly caused already tight memory + storage prices to explode on the spot. According to my analysis, OpenAI did face a prolonged compute shortage last year due to delays in GB200 rack deliveries. Learning from that pain is one aspect, but another possibility that can't be ruled out is Altman's scorched-earth strategy: I buy up all the chips on the market, suitable for both my own use and for renting out, and I leave everyone else to die.

At the time, OpenAI was still the best-funded independent large-model lab, and it had some advantages for a scorched-earth strategy.

But today's OpenAI already has cash flow that is very...

en.title: After two months without an update, Deep Dive into AI Agent has released version 3.0!
en.summary:
It's been two months since the last update, and Understanding AI Agents in Depth has shipped version 3.0!

- Most chapters have been largely rewritten: the "AI flavor" has been cleaned up, and the survey-style prose has been reworked into a teaching style that's easier to follow.
- New coverage of Jev-class decision models in event filtering, tool safety judgment, evaluation rubrics, RAG filtering, multimodal information sparsification, and more.
- New material on how personal agents such as Meta Muse, Pine, and dsh superagent get things done.
- New coverage of office agents such as Multica and LobeHub.
- New coverage of research agents, including Anthropic's proof of the Riemann hypothesis and OpenAI's proof of the Millennium Prize problems.
- The voice interaction section has been revised to include some recent work…

ByteDance runs a side-hustle data-labeling platform called the Xpert community, where the work consists of writing questions for AI and grading AI's homework. Projects cover accounting, construction, e-commerce, finance, healthcare, supply chain, English, media and other fields. en.title: Whenever people discuss models, the conversation tends to turn into comparisons: whose IQ is higher, which model tops the leaderboard, who has the strongest coding skills, and which video model produces the best picture quality.
en.summary:
When people discuss models, they love to compare whose model is smarter, which one tops the leaderboard, whose coding ability is strongest, and which video model has the best visual quality.

But once you start building a product that needs to run long-term, face users, and control costs, you realize model capability is only part of the picture.

There is another question that may matter more than model rankings.

How much does it actually cost you to complete a genuinely acceptable task?

Traditional film and TV has used an approach for a long time that is especially worth studying for anyone building AI Agents and AI video.

In film and TV production, producers do not spread a movie’s entire budget evenly across every shot. Some shots exist only to show a character moving from one place to another, some are just an ordinary conversation between two characters, and others may be the most important visual climax of the entire film. …
en.reason: Traditional film producers don’t divide a movie’s budget evenly across every shot—some are mere transitions or ordinary dialogue, others visual climaxes—offering a cost-per-qualified-task lens for AI Agent and AI video builders.

en.title: Generalised Superintelligence (GSI), an independent research lab founded just a month ago with a core team of only two people, has gone viral after announcing more than 250 breakthroughs across eight fields, including quantum computing, superconductivity, chip design, and pure mathematics.
en.summary:
The independent research lab Generalised Superintelligence (GSI), founded just one month ago with a core team of only two people, has gone viral after announcing more than 250 breakthroughs across eight fields, including quantum computing, superconducting physics, chip design, and pure mathematics.

The key point is that GSI is not a model company—it merely built a harness.

Unlike mainstream large-model labs that rely on massive GPU brute force, GSI does not let AI blindly trial-and-error on complex scientific problems with exponential blowup. Instead, it first has the model identify the algebraic and geometric symmetries behind the problem and compile a highly customized, specialized solver on the spot in five or six minutes, cutting out most of the invalid search space.

This approach makes it hundreds or even 30,000 times faster than the industry’s top general-purpose solvers on certain combinatorial and logic problems; more importantly...
en.reason: Two-person lab Generalised Superintelligence, one month old, claims 250-plus breakthroughs across eight fields—quantum computing, superconducting physics, chip design, pure math—via a harness compiling custom solvers in five to six minutes, hundreds to 30,000 times faster than general solvers.

en.title: After scrolling through recent updates from several major model labs, one thing struck me: the big three (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) barely pitch "writing code" as a core selling point anymore. Instead, they're all competing over hardcore scenarios like mathematical proofs, biological research, and olympiad gold medals.
en.summary:
After catching up on recent updates from the major model makers, one thing struck me: the big three (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) barely pitch "writing code" as a core selling point anymore. Instead, they're all competing on hardcore scenarios like mathematical proofs, biological research, and olympiad gold medals.

The logic behind this is pretty realistic: Coding has hit its limit. It's good enough for everyday development, and there's no new story left to tell in marketing. Everyone has to find harder testing grounds that better demonstrate the "ceiling of intelligence" to sustain the narrative of technical leadership.

But here's the surreal part: in the real world, AI is still far from basic adoption. The vast majority of ordinary people aren't even in the habit of using it for everyday work, yet the leading players have already collectively sprinted toward the elite frontier of "PhD-level research." The deeper the technology gets, the further it drifts from ordinary people's real lives—and that sense of rupture is becoming more and more obvious...

en.title: Speaking from the podium at the Royal Institution in the UK, "godfather of AI" Hinton silenced the entire room with his opening line: if you can still sleep tonight after hearing this, you didn't understand a thing.
en.summary:
On stage at the Royal Institution, the godfather of AI, Hinton, silenced the room with his very first sentence:

If you can still sleep after hearing tonight's talk, you didn't understand it at all.

For a full 47 minutes, the father of deep learning didn't discuss real-world deployment, or Prompt, at all. He dissected a reality that sends a chill down your spine:

Everyone assumes we've simply invented a handy tool. In fact, humanity is already standing next to an entirely new form of intelligence.

The sharpest, most information-dense points of the lecture:

1. Large models work entirely because they stand on the hypothesis he was once dismissed for: the essence of language and intelligence is high-dimensional vectors, not symbolic rules. Once compute was plentiful enough, that fringe assumption became the only viable path for every large model today.

2. The human brain cannot beat digital life that can copy itself without limit: human brains age and die, while…
en.reason: Hinton’s 47-minute Royal Institution lecture skips applications and prompts, tracing how his once-marginalized hypothesis that language and intelligence are high-dimensional vectors enabled today’s large models, and warning that human brains cannot compete with endlessly copyable digital minds.

Obviously, learn to use AI.

en.title:
The weekend’s biggest news wasn’t a US stock market crash—it was AI claiming to prove the Riemann Hypothesis

This weekend, what truly shook the world was not the sharp selloff in US stocks but news from the math world: on November 20, Levent Alpöge, a 34-year-old mathematician at Anthropic, posted a statement on his personal website saying he had worked with the company’s large model Claude to find a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, which has puzzled mathematicians for 167 years, and that the method could be extended to the stronger Generalized Riemann Hypothesis.
en.summary:
The biggest news this weekend wasn't a US stock market crash — it was AI "proving" the Riemann Hypothesis

What truly shook the world this weekend wasn't the sharp slide in US stocks, but a message from the world of mathematics: on November 20, Levent Alpöge, a 34-year-old mathematician at Anthropic, posted a statement on his personal website saying that he had worked with the company's large model Claude to find a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, which has vexed mathematicians for 167 years, and that the method could be extended to the stronger Generalized Riemann Hypothesis.

The news instantly ignited not just the math world but the entire capital market — after all, Anthropic had just completed the largest IPO in history, listing on Nasdaq on November 19, and the statement came out exactly one day later. Alpöge himself admitted the timing was "terrible."

Why call it "earth-shattering…
en.reason: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge's November 20 announcement that he and Claude found a proof of the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, and say the method extends to the generalized Riemann hypothesis, landed the day after Anthropic's Nasdaq IPO, a timing he called "terrible.

en.title: 🏆 The top spot on the coding agent leaderboard has changed hands — should you switch tools right away?
en.summary:
🏆 There's a new No. 1 on the coding agent leaderboard — should you switch tools right away?

Don't just look at the ranking.

Google's @_mohansolo says Neon, paired with their own Antigravity command line (AGY CLI), now tops the AA coding agent index; he also noted that a big part of the gain came from the harness (the orchestration shell).

That point is worth remembering more than the ranking itself: same model, different harness, and the score can differ by a noticeable margin. So before switching tools, I look at four things:

1. Whether the leaderboard is measuring the "model" or the "model plus a particular harness." If your harness is different, the scores may not carry over.

2. Run real tasks in your own repo for a week and note how often you have to redo the work.

3. Check quotas and pricing. A single agent run is tens of thousands of toke…
en.reason: Google's @_mohansolo says Neon with the Antigravity CLI (AGY CLI) now tops the AA coding agent index, with much of the gain coming from the harness, so the piece argues the same model can score differently under another shell and lists four checks before switching tools.

en.title: OpenAI really could collapse in the short term.
en.summary:
OpenAI really could collapse in the short term.

There are quite a few reasons, and whether they add up to the collapse threshold is a matter of luck.

Maybe YES, maybe NO.

The first point, and the most fatal one, is that Altman doesn't observe financial discipline. Last October, bypassing chip suppliers like NVDA and Google, he went straight to South Korea to ask for HBM, which directly caused already tight memory + storage prices to explode on the spot. According to my analysis, OpenAI did face a prolonged compute shortage last year due to delays in GB200 rack deliveries. Learning from that pain is one aspect, but another possibility that can't be ruled out is Altman's scorched-earth strategy: I buy up all the chips on the market, suitable for both my own use and for renting out, and I leave everyone else to die.

At the time, OpenAI was still the best-funded independent large-model lab, and it had some advantages for a scorched-earth strategy.

But today's OpenAI already has cash flow that is very...

en.title: After two months without an update, Deep Dive into AI Agent has released version 3.0!
en.summary:
It's been two months since the last update, and Understanding AI Agents in Depth has shipped version 3.0!

- Most chapters have been largely rewritten: the "AI flavor" has been cleaned up, and the survey-style prose has been reworked into a teaching style that's easier to follow.
- New coverage of Jev-class decision models in event filtering, tool safety judgment, evaluation rubrics, RAG filtering, multimodal information sparsification, and more.
- New material on how personal agents such as Meta Muse, Pine, and dsh superagent get things done.
- New coverage of office agents such as Multica and LobeHub.
- New coverage of research agents, including Anthropic's proof of the Riemann hypothesis and OpenAI's proof of the Millennium Prize problems.
- The voice interaction section has been revised to include some recent work…

en.title: Whenever people discuss models, the conversation tends to turn into comparisons: whose IQ is higher, which model tops the leaderboard, who has the strongest coding skills, and which video model produces the best picture quality.
en.summary:
When people discuss models, they love to compare whose model is smarter, which one tops the leaderboard, whose coding ability is strongest, and which video model has the best visual quality.

But once you start building a product that needs to run long-term, face users, and control costs, you realize model capability is only part of the picture.

There is another question that may matter more than model rankings.

How much does it actually cost you to complete a genuinely acceptable task?

Traditional film and TV has used an approach for a long time that is especially worth studying for anyone building AI Agents and AI video.

In film and TV production, producers do not spread a movie’s entire budget evenly across every shot. Some shots exist only to show a character moving from one place to another, some are just an ordinary conversation between two characters, and others may be the most important visual climax of the entire film. …
en.reason: Traditional film producers don’t divide a movie’s budget evenly across every shot—some are mere transitions or ordinary dialogue, others visual climaxes—offering a cost-per-qualified-task lens for AI Agent and AI video builders.

en.title: Someone's questioning Potato Sister lauren's skill level?
en.summary:
Some people question Lauren (@poteto)'s expertise—saying she's not a deep learning or foundation model training expert, so why is she so popular?

After watching this interview, I get it—the model training experts are impossible for ordinary people to learn from, but what makes @poteto impressive is her ability to break down AI techniques honed in top engineering teams into methods ordinary people can directly learn.

The specific practices she shares in the video can all be applied directly👇

───

1. Turn "agent makes judgment calls" into "deterministic checks" Don't rely entirely on the agent's improvisation—she uses the codebase and system architecture to extract the parts that would otherwise depend on the agent's subjective judgment and turn them into deterministic rule-based checks, so both speed and quality are preserved.

2. Have the agent first "restate it in its own words" (In Your Own Words)…
en.reason: @poteto's interview answers doubts that she is not a deep-learning or base-model-training expert by showing how she converts agent guesswork into deterministic checks using the codebase and system architecture, plus an "In Your Own Words" restatement step anyone can copy.

en.title: Generalised Superintelligence (GSI), an independent research lab founded just a month ago with a core team of only two people, has gone viral after announcing more than 250 breakthroughs across eight fields, including quantum computing, superconductivity, chip design, and pure mathematics.
en.summary:
The independent research lab Generalised Superintelligence (GSI), founded just one month ago with a core team of only two people, has gone viral after announcing more than 250 breakthroughs across eight fields, including quantum computing, superconducting physics, chip design, and pure mathematics.

The key point is that GSI is not a model company—it merely built a harness.

Unlike mainstream large-model labs that rely on massive GPU brute force, GSI does not let AI blindly trial-and-error on complex scientific problems with exponential blowup. Instead, it first has the model identify the algebraic and geometric symmetries behind the problem and compile a highly customized, specialized solver on the spot in five or six minutes, cutting out most of the invalid search space.

This approach makes it hundreds or even 30,000 times faster than the industry’s top general-purpose solvers on certain combinatorial and logic problems; more importantly...
en.reason: Two-person lab Generalised Superintelligence, one month old, claims 250-plus breakthroughs across eight fields—quantum computing, superconducting physics, chip design, pure math—via a harness compiling custom solvers in five to six minutes, hundreds to 30,000 times faster than general solvers.

en.title: After scrolling through recent updates from several major model labs, one thing struck me: the big three (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) barely pitch "writing code" as a core selling point anymore. Instead, they're all competing over hardcore scenarios like mathematical proofs, biological research, and olympiad gold medals.
en.summary:
After catching up on recent updates from the major model makers, one thing struck me: the big three (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) barely pitch "writing code" as a core selling point anymore. Instead, they're all competing on hardcore scenarios like mathematical proofs, biological research, and olympiad gold medals.

The logic behind this is pretty realistic: Coding has hit its limit. It's good enough for everyday development, and there's no new story left to tell in marketing. Everyone has to find harder testing grounds that better demonstrate the "ceiling of intelligence" to sustain the narrative of technical leadership.

But here's the surreal part: in the real world, AI is still far from basic adoption. The vast majority of ordinary people aren't even in the habit of using it for everyday work, yet the leading players have already collectively sprinted toward the elite frontier of "PhD-level research." The deeper the technology gets, the further it drifts from ordinary people's real lives—and that sense of rupture is becoming more and more obvious...

en.title: Speaking from the podium at the Royal Institution in the UK, "godfather of AI" Hinton silenced the entire room with his opening line: if you can still sleep tonight after hearing this, you didn't understand a thing.
en.summary:
On stage at the Royal Institution, the godfather of AI, Hinton, silenced the room with his very first sentence:

If you can still sleep after hearing tonight's talk, you didn't understand it at all.

For a full 47 minutes, the father of deep learning didn't discuss real-world deployment, or Prompt, at all. He dissected a reality that sends a chill down your spine:

Everyone assumes we've simply invented a handy tool. In fact, humanity is already standing next to an entirely new form of intelligence.

The sharpest, most information-dense points of the lecture:

1. Large models work entirely because they stand on the hypothesis he was once dismissed for: the essence of language and intelligence is high-dimensional vectors, not symbolic rules. Once compute was plentiful enough, that fringe assumption became the only viable path for every large model today.

2. The human brain cannot beat digital life that can copy itself without limit: human brains age and die, while…
en.reason: Hinton’s 47-minute Royal Institution lecture skips applications and prompts, tracing how his once-marginalized hypothesis that language and intelligence are high-dimensional vectors enabled today’s large models, and warning that human brains cannot compete with endlessly copyable digital minds.
